articles.title: Looting erupts in Frankfurt as Gen Z protests draw crowds across Germany
articles.summary: By Kai Pfaffenbach, Tilman Blasshofer and Miranda Murray FRANKFURT/BERLIN, Oct 31 (Reuters) - Hooded rioters looted stores in Frankfurt late on Saturday after tens of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets across Germany's biggest cities to demand better education and lower living costs. The protests followed a wave ‌of Gen Z-led demonstrations across Europe this year. In Serbia, student-led activism helped unseat the country's longtime leader at the ballot box, while protests in ‌France have descended into rioting and looting. The German protests organised by the campaign group "Gen Z regelt" — "Gen Z takes charge" in German — took place in 34 cities including Berlin, Frankfurt and Munich. The group says ​it opposes compulsory military service and wants greater investment in education as many young Germans struggle with rising costs. In Frankfurt, Germany's financial hub, at least two stores were looted as protests turned violent, with several more damaged and police trying to get the situation under control, according to a Reuters witness. "Violent disturbances are continuing," Frankfurt police said on X. "In the city centre, windows have been smashed at several shops. Molotov cocktails are also being thrown at the emergency services. We urge all bystanders to avoid the city centre ‌or to leave the area." Official numbers on Saturday afternoon ⁠suggested turnout was below the 182,000 participants that organisers initially expected. Police in Frankfurt, Munich and Berlin reported as many as 18,000 protesters, half the roughly 36,000 on the organisers' website. German authorities said Saturday's demonstrations, which coincide with Halloween festivities, had been largely peaceful, but ⁠warned of attempts by extremist groups to exploit the movement. In Hamburg, some barricades had been set on fire. "We are here today to fight for peace and freedom, rather than for war and coercion," Gen Z regelt spokesperson Lina Friedrich said in Berlin on Saturday. "What matters most to us is better support for the health and education systems. We are against compulsory ​military ​service and we are in favour of a fairer distribution of the burden." LUXURY SHOPS BOARD UP ​WINDOWS Parts of Germany's far-left extremist scene and some groups linked ‌to foreign extremist movements have joined efforts to mobilise support, according to the federal interior ministry. "We all have those images from France in our minds — looting, burning houses, burning police vehicles, and attacks on police officers," said Roman Poseck, interior minister for the state of Hesse, whose capital is Germany's financial hub, Frankfurt. "France must not be held up as a model in this regard." Some businesses across German cities boarded up windows and planned early closures ahead of the demonstrations due to concerns over possible unrest, including along Berlin's luxury Kurfuerstendamm shopping boulevard. Organisers have focused on what they see as the growing pressure on younger generations in Europe's largest economy. "The government has offered no ‌response to our concerns other than to continue making cuts and piling further burdens upon ​us," said Steve, an 18-year-old due to speak at a rally in Munich, addressing Chancellor Friedrich Merz. "We ​will continue to exercise our fundamental right to assemble until you stop ​ignoring us." Germany has struggled to revive economic growth. The country also faces growing pressure on pensions and public services as baby boomers ‌retire and the working-age population shrinks. Questions have been raised about who ​is driving the campaign and whether it ​is genuinely youth-led, given the broad mix of political and civil society groups involved. Germany's national school student umbrella organisation, BSK, has distanced itself from the initiative and plans to hold a separate day of protest on November 20. Sean Baker, a student at the Technical University of Berlin, said he would join ​the protests on Saturday to call attention to the ‌poor state of buildings on campus. "When you go inside and enter the rooms, it looks like an abandoned building," he told Reuters. "Yet this is ​where we're expected to study on a regular basis." (Reporting by Miranda Murray, Timm Reichert, Tilman Blasshofer, Stephan Schepers and Martin Schlicht; Additional reporting ​by Christoph Steitz; Editing by Ros Russell, Joe Bavier, Alex Richardson and David Gregorio) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/gen-z-protests-reach-germany-000319778.html

articles.title: Trump's lawsuit against Wall Street Journal over Epstein letter is dismissed again
articles.summary: Jeffrey Epstein and Donald Trump at Mar-a-Lago in Palm Beach, Florida, on 22 February 1997. Photograph: Davidoff Studios Photography/Getty Images A US judge dismissed Donald Trump’s lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal with prejudice on Saturday, according to a court filing, bringing an end to his legal challenge over the newspaper’s reporting on his alleged birthday letter to Jeffrey Epstein. The decision follows an earlier dismissal in April that had allowed Trump to revise his complaint. As of Saturday, the case is dismissed with prejudice, meaning the lawsuit cannot be amended or refiled. The case stemmed from a Wall Street Journal article alleging that Trump had sent a “bawdy” letter to disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein in 2003. Trump denied the letter was real, insisting instead it had been fabricated. Throughout the proceedings, the court repeatedly pointed to the newspaper’s efforts to obtain Trump’s response before publication and its inclusion of his direct denials as evidence that it had followed appropriate reporting standards. Judge Darrin P Gayles issued the final dismissal on Saturday after determining that Trump’s amended complaint still failed to establish “actual malice”, the high legal threshold public figures must meet when pursuing defamation claims. “As President Trump has not plausibly alleged that each Defendant made defamatory statements with actual malice, the Amended Complaint must be dismissed,” the ruling said. “And because this is President Trump’s second attempt to allege his claims, the Court finds that dismissal with prejudice is appropriate.” Trump, who has frequently pursued legal action against media organizations both during and outside his time in the White House, has maintained that the lewd drawing described in the Journal’s report was fake. A spokesperson for Trump’s legal team shared a statement following the ruling: “President Trump will continue to press forward in his powerhouse lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal and all of the other defendants. The President will continue to hold those who mislead the American People with Fake News and smears accountable for their actions.” A Dow Jones spokesperson said: “We’re pleased with the court’s decision.” Representatives for the Journal had asked the judge to dismiss the claim, arguing that the story was accurate and that it did not meet the bar for defamation. They argued that the reporters had neither knowingly published false information nor proceeded with the belief that the material was likely to be false. The lawsuit attracted particular attention because it named Rupert Murdoch, one of Trump’s most prominent media allies, among the defendants. Murdoch’s News Corporation media empire owns the Journal. Before the article was published on 17 July 2025, Trump personally contacted Murdoch in an effort to stop its publication. The report was published under the headline “Jeffrey Epstein’s Friends Sent Him Bawdy Letters for a 50th Birthday Album. One Was From Donald Trump.” The Journal did not originally publish the image, though it was released by the House oversight committee in September after it was provided by Epstein’s estate. articles.title: What changes when the clocks fall back this weekend
articles.summary: Millions of Americans will gain an hour of sleep this weekend when the twice-a-year time change commonly known as daylight savings ends for 2026. Most of the U.S. will "fall back" an hour when the clocks change at 2 a.m. on Sunday. Here's what to know about what's formally known as daylight saving time as it ends for the year: What is daylight saving time, and why do we have it? Daylight saving time is the period during the year, from March to early November, when the majority of the U.S. operates one hour ahead of standard time. The move effectively "saves" an hour of daylight from the morning and adds it to the evening during the spring and summer months when the days are the longest. In the fall and winter months, when the days are shorter, the U.S. returns to standard time, with daylight coming earlier in the morning. For example, in Boston on Saturday, before the time change, the sun will rise at 7:16 a.m. and set at 5:39 p.m., according to the National Weather Service . On Sunday, back on standard time, sunrise will be at 6:17 a.m. and sunset will be at 4:37 p.m. The U.S. first adopted daylight saving time in 1918 during World War I as an effort to conserve fuel after Europe implemented its own time change, according to the Congressional Research Service . After the war, Congress repealed the clock switch but gave states the option to continue observing it. During World War II and the 1970s energy crisis, Congress brought year-round daylight saving time to the U.S., again with the goal of reducing energy consumption. These experiments didn't last long. After the war, the U.S. let states and municipalities decide for themselves if they wanted to keep daylight saving time and when to observe it. (Congress didn't establish a uniform start and end for the time change until 1966.) In the '70s, continuous daylight saving time was stopped before reaching the 10-month mark. Will the U.S. move to year-round daylight saving time? Earlier this year, legislation to once again make daylight saving time last all year long cleared a major hurdle in Congress. The bill, called the Sunshine Protection Act, passed the House in July and went to the Senate . The legislation would also let states opt out of daylight saving time altogether before the law takes effect. President Trump, who supports the bill, accused a fellow Republican, Arkansas Sen. Tom Cotton, of holding up the legislation . Mr. Trump even posted to social media what he said was Cotton's cellphone number and urged people to call the senator to express their support for the measure. In response, Cotton noted Congress has tried permanent daylight saving time before, only to go back to the twice-yearly time change "once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter." There is a ticking clock for the Senate to take action on the bill. The legislation and any other bills awaiting approval in Congress are set to expire in early January when the new class of lawmakers elected in Tuesday's midterm elections takes office. If the bill does die, the effort to change daylight saving time will have to start over and be approved by the House and the Senate before it can go to the president. Did the time change today? The time won't change until Sunday. For 2026, the end of daylight saving time comes during the overnight hours after Halloween, giving revelers an extra hour of enjoying late-night costume parties — or an extra hour of sleep to recover from their fun. But for parents of young children, the time change can be more of a trick and less of a treat, potentially disrupting their kids' sleep schedules until they adjust. What day and time does daylight saving time end in November 2026? Daylight saving time officially ends at 2 a.m. local time on Sunday, Nov. 1. Americans have been "falling back" on the first Sunday of November since 2007, when the most recent changes to daylight saving time took effect . A 2005 law moved the end date from the last Sunday of October. Do we lose or gain an hour when daylight saving time ends? Most Americans will gain an hour when daylight saving time ends, making up for the hour they lost when the clocks "sprang forward" in March. When will daylight saving time start again in 2027? Daylight saving time is set to begin in 2027 on Sunday, March 14, at 2 a.m. local time. The time change starts on the second Sunday of March, which falls on such a late date next year because the month starts on a Monday. In 2026, daylight saving time started on March 8 . The start date was also changed in 2007 to extend the length of daylight saving time, which previously began on the first Sunday of April. Which states don't do daylight saving time? Daylight saving time is observed in every state except for Hawaii and most of Arizona . The Navajo Nation, which is located in part of Arizona, observes the time change to stay on the same time as their communities in the neighboring states of New Mexico and Utah, according to the tribe . The U.S. territories of American Samoa, Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands also don't observe daylight saving time. Will my phone change for daylight saving time automatically? Phones should change overnight to display the correct time if they're set to update automatically. Apple , Google and Samsung have support pages with instructions for changing the clocks on their devices. Carriers like Simple Mobile and Straight Talk have also posted steps online for checking the settings on other phones. articles.title: D.C. and Virginia sue to stop Trump's massive arch days before construction
articles.summary: The D.C. government and the commonwealth of Virginia sued Saturday to block construction of President Donald Trump’s planned triumphal arch, calling it a “flagrantly unlawful” project that will forever change the landscape of the nation’s capital. The lawsuit is the latest attempt to stop the 250-foot-tall arch, which Trump hopes to build near Arlington National Cemetery and says will commemorate the nation’s 250th birthday. The administration would like to begin construction as soon as next week. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. The two jurisdictions are asking U.S. District Judge Tanya S. Chutkan to halt the plan and argue that they have “indisputable standing” to bring their lawsuit because the towering arch would have tangible, negative effects on the region - an argument that distinguishes their lawsuit from others that have tried to stop Trump’s construction projects. D.C. Attorney General Brian Schwalb (D) said the arch construction would cause “serious, immediate and irreparable harm to the District and its residents,” while Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones (D) said “Trump’s illegal vanity project” would be an affront to Arlington National Cemetery and the “extraordinary sacrifices it represents.” “The Commonwealth has a solemn duty and a profound interest in preserving the dignity of this sacred place,” Jones said in a statement. “We will vigorously litigate to protect its sanctity and honor the legacy of those who made the ultimate sacrifice.” The arch already faces legal peril. In a separate case brought by three Vietnam War veterans and a historic preservationist, Chutkan on Friday signaled she might block it. Asked about the lawsuit, a White House spokesman reiterated the administration’s position that the arch would be “one of the most iconic landmarks” in the world. Spokespeople for the Interior Department, which is managing the project, did not immediately respond to questions about the new lawsuit. The administration has acknowledged that the arch will unavoidably harm local historic sites by altering views, and that it will divert traffic and create loud noise during years of planned construction, among other disruptions. Officials have said that those harms are not significant enough to halt what the administration has deemed a “high-priority project.” The Trump administration has also tried to defend the arch and the president’s other construction projects by claiming that litigants lack standing - the legal grounds to sue - because they cannot show that they would be directly harmed. That argument swayed the Supreme Court this summer in a case about Trump’s White House ballroom. The justices ruled 5-4 that a historic preservationist likely could not prove that she would be harmed by the project - and cleared the way for Trump to keep building. D.C. and Virginia say harms to the region would be irreversible  if Trump’s project proceeds. In their court filing, the jurisdictions argue that the arch would harm the region’s security and emergency preparedness, disrupt traffic, degrade the environment and run afoul of the Height Act, which caps building heights at 130 feet in D.C. - a defining feature of the city’s architecture intended to preserve views of the Washington Monument and the U.S. Capitol. The arch would be nearly double that height. They also say the arch is illegal because Congress has not authorized it, and because the National Park Service failed to follow laws requiring “appropriate consultation before undertaking a project that would transform the District’s physical landscape and upend its historic plan.” The Trump administration has said construction could begin by Thursday if the National Capital Planning Commission - a federal review panel that oversees major projects in the region - approves the arch proposal at its meeting that day. Trump has packed the commission with allies, and its chairman has already said he plans to vote for the project. The Interior Department could then quickly green-light construction, officials have said. Lawyers for D.C. and Virginia argue that if the court fails to act now, the administration could swiftly shift to a new argument - as officials did last year with Trump’s ballroom - that once construction on project begins, it will be too late to stop. “The court should not allow this cynical gambit to succeed,” they wrote in the filing. D.C. Council Chairman Phil Mendelson (D), who has served on the National Capital Planning Commission since 2012, wrote in a declaration to the court that the speed of the commission’s review has been “unprecedented” and insufficient. The commission advanced the proposed arch through key reviews within five weeks, compared with the years-long process to evaluate typical projects, he said. “Congress established a process for approving memorials in Washington for good reason. What we commemorate, where we commemorate it, and how a memorial fits into Washington’s historic landscape are important decisions that deserve careful consideration,” Mendelson said in an accompanying statement. “The proposed Arch has not gone through that process.” Trump has said he hopes to build the arch on Memorial Circle, a traffic roundabout near the south end of Arlington Memorial Bridge and tucked inside Washington’s boundaries. Administration officials have laid out a plan to work 20 hours per day, year-round, for several years to construct the arch. The speed and scope of the president’s project - a planned five-level “concrete structure clad in granite,” as federal officials have described it - have alarmed historic preservationists, architects, parks advocates and local groups that say its effects on the region would be irrevocable. The arch would permanently disrupt historic architectural designs by competing with the Washington Monument, local officials argue. It would also obstruct the sight line between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington House, a memorial to Robert E. Lee. The historic preservation officers from both jurisdictions have raised concerns about a lack of review required by law. But the arch would also cause other logistical headaches, D.C. and Virginia officials say, such as year-round construction for two to three years that would temporarily and permanently change traffic patterns on a busy artery - with potentially serious implications. They note the arch construction could hamper emergency vehicles at the foot of a bridge that is a designated evacuation route. “The construction-related closures of the Circle, new pedestrian crossings, and additional pedestrian and vehicular traffic after construction is finished will all complicate evacuations from and emergency response in the District,” they write. And in a highly restricted airspace, the towering height of the proposed arch would “pose risks to air safety,” which will require local officials to spend significant resources adjusting emergency preparedness plans, D.C. and Virginia officials say. D.C. leaders have not previously sued to block Trump’s construction projects, including the ballroom, the changes to the East Potomac golf course and other projects that have drawn complaints. In a hearing Friday in the separate lawsuit seeking to block the arch, Chutkan independently raised questions about how the arch would affect traffic patterns and other potential disruptions to the region. An administration lawyer told the judge that he was not prepared to talk about traffic patterns because that issue was not germane to that case. Chutkan questioned what harm would be caused by waiting several months versus beginning construction as soon as next week. “What is the rush to put this arch up?” she asked. articles.title: El-Sayed drops former primary rival from Michigan event days before election
articles.summary: Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D) told Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), his once primary opponent, to stay away from his campaign events and disinvited her from a planned appearance on Sunday, a source familiar confirmed to NewsNation, The Hill’s broadcasting partner. The source said El-Sayed does not want the ongoing fight with Stevens to distract from the issues in the final days of his hard-fought Senate campaign. A spokesperson for Stevens did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment. El-Sayed was set to appear alongside Stevens and Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-S.C.) at a church in Detroit, a show of unity despite some harsh words exchanged between the two candidates throughout the week. Stevens released a statement saying she had accepted Clyburn’s invitation to appear alongside El-Sayed, but still criticized the Senate nominee for not condemning an ad that appeared to blame Israel for high grocery prices. “The ad did not invent its argument; it dramatized one Dr. El-Sayed has made in his own words throughout this campaign: that Israel is the reason Michigan cannot afford schools, healthcare, and child care,” Stevens said in her statement. “I therefore expect him to apologize for those statements as well.” The ad was run digitally and was bought by an outside progressive group, not El-Sayed’s campaign. El-Sayed shot back in a statement on Friday, saying Stevens is focused on rehashing their August primary, which he narrowly won. “So while Congresswoman Stevens seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago, let’s all focus on the task at hand: that’s beating Mike Rogers, holding Trump accountable, and getting money out of politics,” El-Sayed said in a statement posted to the social platform X. Support for Israel was a major issue in the Democratic primary. Stevens was backed by millions in funds from pro-Israel lobbying groups, which El-Sayed criticized her for. The Democratic Senate nominee is critical of Israel and has called for the U.S. to stop sending aid to the country. Since the primary, courting Jewish voters has been a hurdle for El-Sayed. His Republican opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers, has worked to earn the support of disaffected Democrats, including those who are Jewish. While Stevens told CNN this week that she still plans to vote for El-Sayed, her fiancé, who is Jewish, announced that he would be voting for Rogers. Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. articles.summary: The Tsaritsyno museum is an imperial palace and park complex in southern Moscow (Mladen ANTONOV) Russia's FSB security service said on Saturday it was carrying out "appropriate" measures after the US embassy in Moscow warned of a planned "terrorist" attack in the capital. The US embassy said earlier it was "aware of a credible threat of a mass casualty event TODAY October 31, at the Tsaritsyno Museum Reserve in Moscow". The US government was "coordinating with appropriate Russian authorities on a response," it said, advising people: "Avoid the area, stay alert, and avoid crowds." The US embassy did not give details on who was plotting the attack. The Tsaritsyno museum is an imperial palace and park complex in southern Moscow that is a popular place to visit, especially on weekends. Russian Telegram channel Baza, which reportedly has links to law enforcement, said the park was now closed and "open only for exits". "Law enforcement officers are on the premises," it reported. Russia's FSB security service said earlier it had received information from the United States "regarding the preparation of a terrorist attack". "Appropriate work is underway," it was quoted as saying by Russian news agencies. The US has provided Russia with warnings of planned attacks before, including in March 2024, weeks before an ISIS-K attack on a Moscow concert hall that killed over 100 people. bur/rmb This article originally appeared on AFP at https://www.yahoo.com/news/world/articles/russia-says-responding-us-report-160743844.html

articles.title: The AI sell-off is exposing the risks of betting on Wall Street’s favorite stocks
articles.summary: Wall Street analysts spent 2026 piling Buy ratings onto the AI build-out. The stocks they ignored have done better. The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) stocks with the biggest share of analyst Buy ratings have trailed those with the smallest share for most of the year, according to Piper Sandler chief investment strategist Michael Kantrowitz. Measured year over year, it's the third-worst stretch in Piper's data going back to 1995. "The Sell Side's MOST favored stocks have underperformed their LEAST favored stocks for the majority of 2026," Kantrowitz wrote in a note to clients Wednesday. This week showed what that looks like. Alphabet had its worst month in history , Intel had its worst day since 1974 , and the Nasdaq ( ^IXIC ) suffered its biggest daily drop since June as Big Tech's results revived worries about AI spending. Add it up, and the AI trade has lost about $5 trillion in market value since Oct. 6, by Yahoo Finance calculations, including about $1.6 trillion on Friday alone. Nvidia and Alphabet, two of Piper's favorites, shed about $835 billion each, roughly a third of the total. Yahoo Finance The rest of the market has held up. The other 625 large US stocks in Yahoo Finance's count gained about $1.3 trillion over the same stretch, led by Eli Lilly ( LLY ), Walmart ( WMT ) and Exxon Mobil ( XOM ). It's the slump in Wall Street's favorites, playing out in a single month. Piper picks both groups from the top and bottom of each of the index's 11 sectors, so this isn't tech against everything else. Only two slumps ran deeper, in 2001-02 and 2010. Both came near big turning points in the market, the first as the tech bubble deflated and the second as stocks recovered from the financial crisis. Piper Sandler, Yahoo Finance Why this hits more portfolios than you'd think Most investors own Wall Street's favorites whether they picked them or not. Nvidia ( NVDA ) and Alphabet ( GOOGL ) are among the biggest weights in the S&P 500, so any index fund or 401(k) that tracks it leans on their fortunes. The slump also shows how a crowded idea can work against investors. When nearly every analyst already loves a stock, much of the good news is in the price, and there are few new buyers left to win over. A disappointment then stings. That's what the favorites are running into. Six of the nine names on Piper's list are down this year, from Alphabet and power producer Vistra ( VST ) to Wynn Resorts ( WYNN ) and Take-Two Interactive ( TTWO ). The exceptions are three AI build-out names: Nvidia, Arista Networks ( ANET ), and Comfort Systems ( FIX ). Meanwhile, nearly all of the least-loved stocks are up, led by steady names like Kenvue ( KVUE ) and Illinois Tool Works ( ITW ). As a group, though, they've only roughly kept pace with the S&P 500. This is less about the laggards running than about the favorites falling. Six of the nine stocks with the most analyst Buy ratings are down this year. Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace A rough week for the AI trade It looked very different in the spring, when Piper's favorites were up nearly 18% on average, by Yahoo Finance calculations. Then the AI trade began to unwind. It crushed the companies leading the data center build-out first, and this week it reached the megacaps. That included the biggest one-day drop in market value in Alphabet's history on Thursday, after its third quarter results. Amazon ( AMZN ) and Intel ( INTC ) led tech lower Friday after their own reports, as Amazon's AI build-out pushed its cash burn to a record . "The AI beta-bubble appears to have already burst!" Kantrowitz wrote. He means the most volatile AI stocks, those with a high beta , which swing more than the market. That doesn't mean the AI trade is over. Kantrowitz expects investors to move toward beaten-down AI companies with stronger businesses as earnings growth slows. In other words, they're getting pickier about which part of AI they pay for. "We do not expect a return to an AI-driven market led by the most speculative (i.e., lower quality) stocks," Kantrowitz wrote. articles.title: Gov. Abbott's political machine faces a major test as Democrats gain ground in Texas
articles.summary: HOUSTON, Texas — On the first day of early voting in Texas, two weeks before the most consequential election Texas Republicans have faced in a generation, Greg Abbott addressed a sweaty crowd of hundreds of supporters packed inside an imitation saloon. The Texas governor pulled out a piece of paper from his pocket. “Steve Radack Community Center, 18650 Clay Road, Houston, 1.2 miles away,” he read, identifying the precinct’s nearest polling location. “Listen, I can roll over there in five minutes,” said Abbott, who uses a wheelchair, as the fawning audience laughed. Abbott was making a closing pitch to the Republican Party’s most fanatic supporters, many donning “Make America Texas” hats, who clapped loudly as he bragged about bringing 2.6 million jobs to Texas and booed at the mention of his “crazy" opponent, Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa. And they perked up when Abbott asked if they wanted to “be your own political power broker and make sure that you’re the one responsible for us winning.” That’s when the governor issued another set of directions: Download the Abbott Impact App, the engine of the massive turnout operation that has enabled the GOP to build tremendous power over Abbott’s nearly 12 years in Austin. Many in the audience dutifully complied. The app is the key to Abbott’s ability to maintain his grip on the most influential red state in the nation through his extensive data, polling and “get out the vote” operation — powerful tools that have not only allowed him to sail to reelection repeatedly but has cemented GOP control of every single statewide office. That could all change in a matter of days. Abbott expected to spend 2026 in legacy mode, cruising to a fourth term that would carry him into the post-Trump era as one of the most dominant state-level GOP figures in America, a kingmaker in a party looking for new heroes. Instead, he’s fighting a tougher-than-expected battle to retain his own seat, under weight from the unpopular war in Iran and rural blowback to data centers, Flock cameras and school vouchers. His longtime ticketmate, Attorney General Ken Paxton, is facing an even more arduous challenge in his attempt to keep the state’s U.S. Senate seat in Republican hands. A victory by Democrat James Talarico would crack a three-decade lockout from power in Texas for his party, and potentially redraw the national map ahead of the 2028 presidential election. Texas Republicans who have lost confidence in Paxton as a candidate, and are worried about the sour national mood more broadly, are now banking on Abbott’s finely tuned, expansive GOTV political machine to save the party. Ultimately, the election will reveal whether even the most powerful political force in Texas can fall — and determine what becomes of the Texas GOP if voters deliver a blow to the heart of American conservatism. “Paxton’s going to win the race,” Abbott told reporters in Austin in October as he kicked off a mad campaigning dash across the state, in response to being asked by POLITICO Magazine who gets the blame should Paxton lose. “So the real question is who gets the credit for it.” Not long ago there was a time when Abbott could clearly claim such credit. There’s arguably no Republican in America who has done more to nurture and benefit from the populist MAGA energy that President Donald Trump has unleashed over the past decade than Abbott. He has been able to navigate the yawning divisions between the two wings of the GOP by carefully riding the rise of the far right while also maintaining the respect of old school country club Republicans. That formula didn't work for Sen. John Cornyn, who found himself on the wrong side of MAGA a few too many times to maintain the fragile marriage of GOP factions and was ousted by Paxton in this year’s primary. Yet Abbott has deftly managed the party’s splintering, perhaps better than any other Republican whose rise pre-dated Trump. The question now is whether he can still motivate the base with the same intensity he’s done again and again. Even though most Texas Republicans — and many Democrats as well — quickly dismiss the scenario that Abbott himself could lose, public polling consistently shows Hinojosa within striking distance. Abbott has alienated rural voters over his staunch support for data centers and school vouchers , while his ties to megabillionaires have fueled a Democratic campaign that casts the election as a referendum on corruption as much as affordability. Meanwhile, some establishment Republicans have grown weary of the party’s fixation on culture-war battles that Abbott himself has helped stoke, particularly in an election where voters say they care more about the economy. It remains to be seen whether Abbott’s GOTV operation can surge turnout despite those headwinds. “He was the coattails for every cycle as governor,” said a senior Republican Texas official, granted anonymity to speak freely about the state’s dominant GOP leader. “He got people over the finish line in difficult House seats and Senate seats and congressional seats. He was the man.” This cycle, the official said, “Abbott has no coattails.” Texans of both parties say they’ve seen this scenario before: An abrasive, flamethrowing Republican is in the fight of his political life against a charismatic, rising-star Democrat who has reignited the party’s hopes of ending their decades-long losing streak in Texas by flipping a Senate seat. Faced with the limitations of his own ground game, the Republican leans on Abbott’s massive field operation to churn out votes, an organization powered by an army of thousands of volunteers and advanced data metrics. In 2018, Abbott’s operation helped Ted Cruz beat Beto O’Rourke by about 219,000 votes, running up the score in rural areas and turning out unreliable Republican voters. Cruz’s team saw the gap in the data: Abbott had a far broader coalition and a statewide field team that could help Republicans weather the unprecedented Democratic turnout O’Rourke was driving. The governor easily won his race by 13 points. “He’s feared because of a very effective organization,” said Bill Noble, a former senior adviser to Abbott’s predecessor, former Texas GOP Gov. Rick Perry. “It’s better to be on the side of having the governor endorsing you, and with that endorsement comes more than just a press release. Money’s made available, lists and resources are made available [and] delivering the vote after the endorsement.” Abbott’s hope is that the 2018 magic that saved Cruz can play out in the final years of the Trump era for Paxton, even with his party in transition. But the barriers facing the GOP — and Abbott himself — are far stronger this time around. Sure, Abbott can give Paxton a ground game. But can he turn Abbott voters into Paxton voters? And more to the point: Are there as many Abbott voters as there were in 2018? Meanwhile, after decades of being outgunned by Republicans, Democrats are working on building their own turnout machine. Brazoria County is the blueprint. Stretching from Houston to the Gulf Coast, this county has been run almost entirely by Republicans since the Republic of Texas was established in 1836. It’s the former political home base of the libertarian-leaning Republican Ron Paul and hotbed of the Tea Party movement before its reactionary politics went national in 2010. Therefore the odds are daunting for the small group of Democrats who, in 2025, devised a plan to mount a coordinated campaign within Brazoria County to assemble strength from the bottom up. The Brazoria project grew out of a statewide coordinated campaign launched this year by a coalition of Democratic groups who have invested $30 million in an effort to end the party’s 30-year drought in winning higher office. The experiment is targeting Brazoria this midterm and if successful, Democrats plan to replicate it across the state the next cycle. Texas Democrats have long yearned for year-round, state-wide campaign infrastructure. That burden typically falls on the Democrat at the top of the ticket to build out themselves, as in 2018 when O’Rourke created a massive, decentralized GOTV operation that relied on armies of volunteers. But after he lost, it evaporated. This cycle’s statewide coordinated campaign running in tandem with the Brazoria project intends to copy-and-paste that strategy but in a permanent way that will exist after the fumes of the 2026 election dissipate. Democrats believe the ingredients in Brazoria are all there, a microcosm of the story of Texas’ demographic growth over the last decade. Over the past 15 years, new residents from both inside and outside Texas have poured into the region, drawn by good schools, plentiful jobs and proximity to a major city — and by the promise of planting roots in the massive master-planned communities that have become a hallmark of Texas living. Brazoria’s growth is reshaping not just its suburbs but its demographics. Hispanic residents now make up about 32% of the county’s population, while Black residents account for roughly 18% and Asian residents nearly 9%. Those demographics work in Democrats’ favor: Enraged by ICE’s aggressive immigration enforcement under Trump, Latino voters are rapidly moving away from the GOP after a record number of them supported the president in 2024. But Texas Democrats are learning that demographics alone won’t deliver them power without some grit. The idea, Texas Majority PAC’s Katherine Fischer said, was to borrow from Republicans’ 1980s playbook: invest in rural, Democratic-leaning counties that were beginning to trend Republican — just the reverse. Brazoria caught their attention as they observed it shifting bluer cycle after cycle, although Democratic gains stalled slightly in 2024 when Trump won it by 20 points. They wanted to accelerate that shift, starting by recruiting a full slate of candidates for the first time. Republicans have so dominated the state’s politics that Democrats in the past didn’t even bother to field candidates in many down-ballot races. The Texas Democratic Party and Texas Majority PAC decided to fill every seat in Brazoria and partnered with County Democratic Chair Monica Morgan to make that happen. Those groups poured $450,000 into the project — hiring staff, paying for an office and covering the thousands of dollars in filing fees that dissuades potential candidates from making the leap. Candidates were then given one-on-one training through Texas Majority PAC, which provided campaign strategy, fundraising support, voter-data guidance and canvassing help. “[The PAC is] really pushing us in a healthy way to be successful,” said Becky Singleton, a Democrat running for county commissioner. “It took my own campaign to a whole new level.” The slate of Brazoria Democrats, who have become close friends throughout the cycle, got an early jolt of inspiration: In May, Democrat Quentin Wiltz flipped Brazoria’s biggest city of Pearland, winning by 263 votes in a city of about 130,000. For them it was a sign that Democrats had a chance to prevail, even in a county Trump carried by a wide margin. “We have millions of people in Texas who historically have been under-engaged,” Wiltz said. “When you give people a reason to participate and organize, and then when you have the resources to invest in them, you can reach them and you can see the change that’s possible.” Brazoria Republicans, in the face of a real opposition this year, are digging in. They’re even consolidating behind a deceased judicial candidate who died in September. Should the candidate win next week, the GOP-controlled board of county commissioners will appoint his replacement. (The Democrat in the race, Shenequa Harrison, makes the case that “if you vote for him, you literally you don't know who you're voting for.”) Democrats’ ambition now is to scale this model dramatically, with organizers saying they could recruit and support three times as many local candidates next cycle. “If we see that the experiment in Brazoria seems to be successful, we can then export that experiment to other counties across the state,” Fischer said, pointing to rapidly growing Kaufman County outside Dallas and the heavily Hispanic Rio Grande Valley as potential next targets. “We're not going to win overnight, but we will win one day, and we want to speed it up and make sure that we have good people in these seats when we do actually win.” Many Texas Republicans see Abbott’s GOTV dominance as an expression of his reputation as a hardworking overachiever with an intense obsession with detail. That reputation is in part a result of his biography: As a 26-year-old law firm associate studying for the bar, he was out for a jog when in a freak accident, a tree fell on him, leaving the lower half of his body paralyzed. The accident didn’t halt his meteoric rise from attorney to judge to state attorney general to governor. “He’s tenacious,” GOP state Sen. Paul Bettencourt said. “Incredibly disciplined,” said Republican state Rep. Greg Bonnen. “He has overcome a tremendous amount of adversity,” state Sen Phil King said. Abbott’s campaign knew that this would be a tough election year, so his aides adjusted their GOTV strategy. “We increased the targets and we increased the universe,” Dave Carney, Abbott’s top political adviser, told me. Rather than begin canvassing immediately after the primary, as it had during his previous reelection bid, the team held back its volunteers until the fall, betting that voter contact would be more effective once the race was on voters’ radar. Those volunteers — about 10,000 — have identified 3 million potential voters through the Abbott Impact App by uploading their contacts and matching them to voter files to confirm party affiliation and determine if they have voted. The app gamifies voter outreach, which occurs either through text or door knocks, and rewards top users with prizes like a Traeger grill, Dyson blowdryer or private tour of the governor’s mansion. “It’s basically a field operation on your phone,” Carney said. Abbott’s team insists they’re still focused on the governor’s goal of flipping seats in Harris County, which includes Houston and has a history of swinging between parties although it is currently Democratic-run. Abbott has devoted more than $30 million of his war chest to the effort. In 2024 Republicans successfully flipped several Harris judicial races and this year they’re eyeing races toward the top of the ballot like county judge — which would amount to an exceptional coup in a difficult year. “Any vote we pull out of Harris County is going to help the statewide ticket,” said Jessica Colon, Abbott’s senior adviser running the field operation in Harris County. “If it’s a voter numbers contact game, we’ve got ‘em smashed with that,” said Jeff MacGeorge, a district field director in Harris County, who said his team has sent more than 3.5 million texts to voters since the primary and 2,000 people in the county have downloaded the app. Republican state Rep. Gary Gates, who represents a district in the Houston area, said he opens the Abbott Impact App every Monday morning to see how many blocks the governor’s volunteers walked the weekend before, efforts the four-term Republican says he has never seen as organized or extensive. In one week in October the Abbott team knocked on more than 5,300 doors and completed 1,300 voter surveys in his Fort Bend County district, he said. But even with those efforts, Gates is pessimistic about how Republicans will fare next week given the negative national environment. After all, knocking on a voter’s door does not ensure they will show up at the polls for your side. “You just can’t go tick off and declare war on the Latinos and not have it come back and bite you in the rear end,” Cates said. “That’s going to have consequences.” Early vote returns signaled some warning signs for Republicans, with Democrats showing up in slightly higher numbers while rural voter turnout is lagging . Of course, those dynamics can quickly reverse, a possibility Texas House Speaker Dustin Burrows is betting on, thanks largely to Abbott. “Many of them believe Election Day is the right day to vote,” he said. “So I expect us to have a huge Election Day for Republicans.” Burrows was doing his part, participating in a cross-state bus tour to mobilize Republicans: “It feels really good on the ground,” he told me. “It feels a whole lot better than what it sounds like on Twitter.” That confidence in the rural firewall is not shared among all Republicans, particularly with Abbott’s biggest detractors within the party. Former GOP state Rep. Glenn Rogers — whom Abbott successfully chased from office in his vendetta against lawmakers who opposed his school voucher push — said he’s had many conversations with Republicans in his small town of Graford indicating slipping support for the governor. Abbott’s efforts to attract data centers to Texas — which he dialed back following backlash — coupled with private school advocacy has alienated those supporters and promoted a “distrust” of him, Glenn said. A Republican defeat next week might trigger a recalibration within the party away from the culture wars and toward bread-and-butter economic issues, he said. “It’d be the best thing that could happen to them,” Glenn predicted. “I don’t see any change occurring in the Republican Party unless they get their ass whipped in November.” Back at the saloon in Houston, after Abbott concluded his remarks, a long line of fans waited to snap a photo with him before being rushed aside by an attentive staffer. Standing on the outskirts of the crowd stood a retired rancher from the border town of Brownsville, a longtime Republican in a family of other longtime Republicans who cast a ballot as soon as the polls opened. Asked about recent polls showing Hinojosa within a few points of Abbott, the rancher, who declined to share his name, dismissed them as “driven by Democrats.” And questioned about how he thinks his party will fare next week, he shrugged. “It’s Texas,” he said. articles.title: Democratic candidates criticize Biden's border record in push to win swing voters
articles.summary: James Talarico; Adam Hamilton; Paige Cognetti. (USA Today Network; Reuters; Getty) WASHINGTON — Democratic candidates in 2026 battleground races are directly criticizing Joe Biden’s handling of border security when he was president, seeking to neutralize a political vulnerability and signaling a new path for the party on the thorny issue. Candidates are throwing the ex-president under the bus on border policy in key states that will decide control of the Senate and some battleground House races across the country. “I called out Joe Biden for failing us on the border,” Texas’ Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico says in a recent ad airing in the closing stretch of his neck-and-neck race against Republican Ken Paxton. He also criticized Biden in July for having “failed us on our southern border” as he rolled out his own border security plan . He’s not alone. In Kansas, a longtime Republican stronghold, Democrat Adam Hamilton criticized Biden in a recent debate with Republican Sen. Roger Marshall. “I want to be crystal clear, first of all: Immigration at the border under Biden was a disaster. That is how we ended up where we are today,” he said. “Second, what we did in response to that has been a disaster for people across the state of Kansas.” Hamilton, like other Democrats in areas that voted for Trump in 2024, paired their critique of Biden with criticism that the current president has gone too far on enforcement. Polls show many Americans have soured on Trump’s handling of the issue in the wake of immigration officers fatally shooting two Americans in Minnesota and one in Maine this year. Still, the comments reflect a recognition that the issue of border security remains a vulnerability for Democrats as Republicans continue to accuse them of promoting “open borders” in a bid to mobilize their base and win swing voters. Biden’s ratings on the issue tanked amid a surge in migrant crossings during his presidency, which Trump successfully weaponized in 2024. Entering office in 2021, Biden inherited a Covid-era migration surge that intensified in the United States after he made good on his pledge to roll back Trump-era policies and restrictions, allowing more asylum-seekers to stay in the country as their cases were being considered. The collective result was a huge spike in border crossings that became associated with the Biden presidency and brought down his approval ratings. Even as Trump’s approval rating has fallen to 38% , polls show border security continues to be one of his highest-polling issues, although that number has fallen from the highs of his early second term. “The Biden administration failed at the border,” Democratic House candidate Paige Cognetti said at a debate Thursday night. Cognetti, who is vying to unseat Rep. Rob Bresnahan, R-Pa., in a highly competitive Scranton-area working-class district, later added: “The Biden administration did fail. We need to make sure that the border is secure. It’s a good thing that it is. We do need to make sure that the pathways to citizenship are there.” In South Carolina, Democratic Senate candidate Annie Andrews said in a debate, “Democrats have failed on the border.” Democratic pollster Celinda Lake said it’s “very smart” for candidates to distance themselves from Biden and that “there’s nobody contesting that interpretation” that he blundered on the border. In the 2024 election, “immigration was playing a major, major role, and it was energizing Republicans. And it was the best issue among swing voters for Republicans,” she said. “ICE has gone too far, and that has backfired now.” She added that the “best messaging” on immigration is “some control for the border plus a humanitarian process for immigration.” Iowa’s Democratic Senate candidate Josh Turek traveled more than 800 miles to Laredo, Texas, to film an ad at the border touting his support for tougher enforcement. “I came to the border to meet firsthand with the people who work to keep it secure. What happens down here affects us up in Iowa, so we’ve got to address it,” Turek says in the ad . “I voted with Republicans to allow law enforcement to arrest and deport criminals.” Weeks earlier, he released another ad speaking to Iowans and vowing that he would “work with anyone” to fix immigration — “including President Trump, to secure the border.” Closer to the border, Democrat Johnny Garcia is trying to win Texas’ redrawn and Republican-friendly 35th Congressional District against GOP nominee Carlos De La Cruz. Garcia criticized Trump’s ICE raids as detrimental to the economy. But at a recent forum , he also blamed Biden’s policies for failures at the border and referred to a fatal smuggling conspiracy in 2022 that led to the deaths of dozens of people. “We’ve also gotten to see, unfortunately, how Biden got it wrong on the border,” Garcia said. “I’ll admit that every single day. We got to see one of the largest migrant fatalities in this district in south San Antonio, with 53 migrants that were locked in a trailer.” “So we can’t afford to just turn a blind eye to our border,” he added. “But at the same time, we can’t turn a blind eye to what we’re seeing happening on our streets.” This article was originally published on NBCNews.com This article originally appeared on NBC News at https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-election/2026-democratic-candidates-throw-joe-biden-bus-border-security-rcna603228

articles.title: “中选决战”在即，为避免被横扫，共和党要保“基本盘”
articles.summary: 美国中期选举进入最后冲刺阶段，共和党正面临近年来最严峻的选情压力。民调显示，民主党在国会通用选票上领先逾8个百分点， 众议院大概率易手，参议院亦岌岌可危，共和党人正在全力防守本应稳固的深红阵地。 据媒体报道，参选双方策略师和民调专家普遍认为，民主党夺回共和党主导的众议院胜算较大——特朗普执政以来民调支持率持续下滑，选民对生活成本上涨及伊朗战争的不满情绪持续发酵。最新民调显示，特朗普支持率仅为40%，不满意度高达59%，创该媒体中期选举相关调查自1990年以来的最高纪录。参议院方面，共和党目前以53比47占优，但民主党正在阿拉斯加、俄亥俄、德克萨斯等红州发起冲击。 对市场而言，国会权力格局的潜在转变意味着特朗普政策议程将面临更大阻力，财政支出走向、贸易政策及监管环境的不确定性或将随之上升。无党派选情观察机构Inside Elections在过去一周调整了64场众参两院及州长竞选的评级，其中63场对民主党有利，仅1场对共和党有利。 深红区告急，共和党被迫全面防守 共和党焦虑情绪最直观的体现，是其防守资源向本不应出现争议的选区大举倾斜。 据媒体报道，本月早些时候一项民调显示，共和党候选人Anthony Constantino在纽约一个农村选区落后民主党对手4个百分点——而该选区在2024年曾以21个百分点的优势支持特朗普。共和党操盘手Roger Stone随即向白宫示警，建议安排副总统JD Vance赴当地出席造势活动，以巩固MAGA基本盘，守住即将退休的众议员Elise Stefanik留下的席位。Vance随后将该选区列入大选前最后一天的行程。 Cook Political Report预测，最有可能的结果是民主党在新一届众议院中获得227至240席（总席位435席），而共和党目前多数席位仅为219比214。众议院民主党竞选委员会近期持续向更安全的共和党选区加大投入，显示民主党对扩大战场版图更具信心。 关键选民群体流失，共和党基本盘出现裂痕 《纽约时报》基于其选民趋势数据及对七个参议院关键州的最新民调，梳理出令共和党深感忧虑的选民结构变化。 无大学学历白人选民是特朗普时代共和党的核心支柱，但在绝大多数战场州，共和党参议院候选人的得票率均明显落后于特朗普2024年的胜选幅度。由于该群体在德克萨斯州和阿拉斯加州以外的每个战场州均占多数，哪怕温和的流失也会产生重大影响。近期民调显示，共和党在该群体中的支持率已出现两位数的下滑，这也是阿拉斯加和堪萨斯等传统红州今年被纳入竞争之列的主要原因之一。 年轻选民方面，共和党2024年在30岁以下群体中几乎与民主党持平，但最新民调显示，民主党目前在这一群体中领先超过33个百分点。2024年共和党在30岁以下男性群体中领先24个百分点，而2026年民调显示民主党已在此群体中反超，领先9个百分点。 德克萨斯州西裔选民的逆转同样引人瞩目。2024年共和党在该州西裔中小幅胜出，但2026年最新民调显示，民主党候选人James Talarico在西裔群体中领先32个百分点，较2024年实现了33个百分点的巨大逆转。若民主党赢得德克萨斯州参议院席位，将是该党三十余年来首次在该州取得全州范围的胜利。 参议院战场犬牙交错，各方押注"例外" 在参议院战场中，共和党并非毫无亮点。 缅因州参议员Susan Collins是共和党在艰难选情下的异类。她长期以温和共和党人形象示人，历来能够争取独立选民和民主党选民支持。民调显示，Collins在45岁及以上女性群体中的表现显著优于共和党整体水平——这一群体在2024年大选中以两位数优势支持民主党，但目前民调显示Collins仍占优势。缅因州也是今年顶级参议院战场中唯一一个特朗普在2024年未能赢得的州。 爱荷华州方面，共和党众议员Ashley Hinson正在争夺一个参议院空缺席位，选情胶着。她已在竞选中公开与特朗普的政策主张保持距离。当被问及是否同意特朗普所称美国目前拥有"A++++++经济体"时，Hinson在ABC新闻节目上直言："现在感觉可不像。" 阿拉斯加方面，本周民主党候选人Mary Peltola的团队曾运作引入"搅局候选人"，特朗普政府和该州共和党籍州长随即启动调查，共和党将此视为难得的翻盘契机。 候选人各自为战，党内战略分歧浮现 选情压力下，共和党内部开始出现明显的策略分化。 据媒体报道，在亚利桑那州一个涵盖凤凰城和斯科茨代尔部分地区的高度竞争众议院选区，共和党候选人Jay Feely已悄然调整竞选形象——原本写有"特朗普背书"的竞选标牌，已被换成"警察背书"。 众议院多数党领袖Steve Scalise（共和党，路易斯安那州）呼吁候选人走出去帮助五五开选区的同僚，而非沉浸于对选情的焦虑。"很多人焦虑，是因为他们看电视，看到各种末日预言，我认为部分内容是为了打压共和党的投票率，"他表示。 特朗普本人则密集举行造势集会，并多次前往本应稳妥的共和党腹地。他将此次中期选举定性为"逆风翻盘"的叙事，声称自己将打破执政党中期选举通常失利的历史规律。白宫发表声明称，特朗普"是共和党无可争议的领袖、最佳传播者和无与伦比的激励者，致力于维持共和党在国会的多数地位"。 不过，媒体援引知情人士称，特朗普近日情绪趋于低落，在两周密集巡回造势后声音已明显嘶哑。当被问及如何应对民主党控制国会的局面时，他向记者回应称："我们会想办法——我有强有力的否决权。" 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: Marvell收购Lumentum：“芯片 + 光学”的首次深度闭环，“既当裁判又当运动员”与光通信的“赢家通吃”
articles.summary: 10月28日，彭博报道称，Marvell正与光学器件制造商Lumentum进行深入谈判，考虑通过全股票交易收购后者。报道当时给出的Lumentum市值约为830亿美元，Marvell约为2210亿美元。 这笔潜在交易引发了一个值得关注的问题：一家以定制芯片和高速互连见长的公司，为什么要大举进入激光器和光学器件制造领域？ 10月30日，半导体行业播客Semi Doped邀请市场研究机构Cignal AI的两位分析师Andrew Schmitt和Scott Wilkinson讨论这笔交易。两人的判断是，Marvell希望通过垂直整合，把DSP、激光器和光学组件结合起来，形成更完整的产品体系。 如果交易完成，Marvell可能成为少数同时覆盖DSP、激光器和光模块多个环节的企业。但这也会带来新的竞争关系：它一边向光模块厂商供应芯片，一边可能进入这些客户的市场。 一、从DSP到激光器、光模块：Marvell想打通整条链 主持人提出，Marvell收购Lumentum后，可能成为一家同时拥有DSP、激光器和光模块业务的公司。Andrew Schmitt认为，最接近这一模式的先例是Acacia，但Marvell与Lumentum的组合在业务规模和覆盖范围上可能更进一步。 他首先澄清，Marvell并不缺激光器供应。公司目前主要为ZR相干模块采购可调谐激光器，与多家供应商保持着良好关系。收购Lumentum的核心驱动力，是垂直整合。 Andrew认为，在技术快速变化的市场中，企业需要同时掌握芯片和光学技术，才能更好地控制产品开发和供应链。两类技术放在同一家公司内部，可以协同设计，做出性能更好的产品，也能通过销售更完整的方案获得更多毛利。 Lumentum自身已经有类似的业务组合。Andrew举例，公司此前收购Cloud Light，进入基于硅光技术的数据通信光模块市场。Cloud Light生产的光模块使用Lumentum自己的激光器，同时还需要从Marvell、Broadcom等公司采购PAM4 DSP。 在一只光模块中，激光器和DSP几乎构成了最主要的价值部分，剩下的环节主要是组装。 这意味着，Marvell与Lumentum的业务本来就存在上下游联系。收购完成后，Marvell有机会将原本需要外部采购的关键组件纳入内部体系，进一步整合DSP、激光器和光学引擎。 Andrew认为，这种模式的价值还体现在利润上。 过去，芯片公司的毛利率可能达到50%，光学组件厂商却只有25%至30%。芯片公司自然不愿意收购一家毛利率更低的企业，担心拉低自身利润率。 但他表示，如今光学组件行业的毛利率已经从约25%上升至接近50%。Lumentum在200G EML、光电路交换机（OCS）和高功率激光器等产品上拥有稀缺技术，议价能力也明显增强。 “如果你能赚到更多的钱，只不过这些钱占总收入的比例低一些，那又有什么关系？” Andrew认为，投资者过去过于看重毛利率百分比，忽视了企业能够创造的毛利额。将组件整合成更完整的产品，即使合并后的毛利率比例有所变化，也可能创造更多利润。 他还提到，Marvell六七年前可能只需约30亿美元就能收购Lumentum，如今潜在交易规模可能达到当年的30倍。这是他的回忆和估算，却也反映出光学组件在AI时代的价值变化。 二、既当“裁判”又当“运动员”：Marvell可能与客户竞争 垂直整合会让Marvell获得更完整的产品线，也会改变它与客户的关系。 Scott Wilkinson指出，Marvell目前的相干DSP被大量光模块厂商采用。以400G相干模块为例，除Acacia、Ciena、Nokia以及部分中国厂商外，很多企业都会采购Marvell的DSP。 如果Marvell收购Lumentum，进一步进入光学引擎和模块市场，它就可能与这些原有客户直接竞争。 这正是交易中一个微妙的地方：Marvell既是产业链上游的芯片供应商，也可能成为下游产品的参与者。客户难免会考虑，未来是否还要继续依赖一家与自己竞争的公司提供关键芯片。 主持人Austin提出了一个直接的问题：如果客户因此转向Broadcom、Credo等其他DSP供应商，Marvell是否愿意牺牲部分芯片市场份额，换取光模块业务？ Andrew认为，这是一笔可以计算的商业账： “通过垂直整合，我能够获得比单独销售零部件更多的价值，即使这意味着我可能会少卖一些零部件。” Scott也提醒，真正需要观察的是Marvell如何管理收购后的业务。Lumentum本来就向外部客户销售激光器，也经营部分光模块业务。收购完成后，Marvell未必会把这些产能全部留给自己。 Andrew则认为，客户是否流失，取决于Marvell能否给原有DSP客户和Lumentum的光学客户足够的信心，让他们相信原有供货关系不会受到影响。 这也是垂直整合的代价：企业获得了更多产业链控制权，同时也可能让客户重新寻找供应商。 三、光通信的“赢家通吃”：先发优势不如百万级交付 除了垂直整合，两位分析师还谈到了光通信行业另一个鲜明的竞争规律：新技术标准的市场最终往往由少数厂商占据。 Andrew把这一现象称为“IEEE彩票”。 每当行业推出一项新标准，通常会有五六家公司同时开发产品。几年之后，真正占据大部分出货量的往往只剩两家公司，合计拿下80%至90%的市场份额。 因此，率先推出产品固然重要，但能否抓住市场形成初期的机会，才决定了企业能否成为最终赢家。 Scott进一步指出，当前AI光通信市场的竞争尤其看重产能。 “如果你第一个进入市场，却只能生产一万个，实际上没有太大意义。如果你第二个进入市场，却能够生产一百万个，那么订单就会落到你手里。” 他以中国厂商Eoptolink（光迅科技）为例。这家公司在800G以太网光模块市场进入时间稍晚于部分竞争对手，却凭借产能优势成为全球主要供应商之一。Scott认为，1.6T产品也正在出现类似的竞争局面。 这也是Lumentum受到关注的原因。Scott提到，公司过去几年持续扩大磷化铟（InP）制造能力，产能经历了多轮翻倍式扩张，但市场需求增长更快，仍然难以满足所有客户需求。 Lumentum的优势还在于拥有一些竞争对手难以迅速复制的产品。Andrew特别提到200G EML、OCS和高功率激光器。 他提醒，很多公司都可以宣称自己能够开发出类似产品，但真正的考验是能否从生产几百件扩大到五万件、甚至一百万件。“做出一百个和做出一百万个，完全是两回事。” AI时代，这种规模优势被进一步放大。Andrew认为，光学组件的价值也发生了变化：在传统电信网络中，激光器主要帮助运营商增加传输容量；在AI数据中心中，1.6T互联可能让AI集群训练速度提高两到三倍。 当一项光学技术能够显著提升整个计算集群的效率，客户愿意为它支付的价格自然会发生变化。 四、Nvidia会不会加入竞购？ 访谈最后，两位分析师讨论了Nvidia是否可能成为潜在买家。 Nvidia此前已分别向Lumentum和Coherent投资20亿美元，并与两家公司建立战略合作。Andrew认为，Nvidia同样有垂直整合的动力：此前收购Mellanox，就是为了把网络技术纳入自身GPU系统。如果继续向光学组件和OCS领域延伸，也符合这一思路。 Andrew还提出一种可能性：Marvell与Lumentum的谈判消息如果是有意泄露，或许是在向其他潜在买家释放信号，最终引发竞购战。 不过，他明确表示自己没有交易内幕，这只是个人推测。Nvidia此前的投资和采购合作，也不能证明它有意参与收购。 对Marvell来说，这笔交易的核心考验最终仍是如何平衡两件事：通过整合芯片与光学技术获得更高的整体价值，同时避免原有客户因为竞争关系而转向其他供应商。 Andrew Schmitt的判断是，光学组件已经成为AI基础设施中价值更高的环节，芯片公司收购光学企业的经济逻辑正在改变。Scott Wilkinson则提醒，在光通信这个容易出现“赢家通吃”的市场，产能和规模决定最终份额。 Marvell想打通从芯片到光学的产业链，能否同时守住客户、技术和市场份额，将决定这场整合究竟能创造多大价值。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 为何10月PMI偏弱？
articles.summary: 事件： 10月31日，国家统计局公布10月PMI指数，制造业PMI为49.3%、前值50.1%；非制造业PMI为49.7%、前值50.2%。 1. 核心观点：10月PMI偏弱，不仅与假期效应退坡有关，也反映高油价、AI产业调整影响 制造业PMI： 10月PMI回落幅度持平2022年以来的偏弱季节性，主要源于假期效应退坡的影响，一是表现为“抢生产”结束。 10月制造业PMI回落0.8个百分点至49.3%，与2022年以来偏弱的季节性一致(环比-0.8%)。主要分项看，前月在假期备货影响下，生产指数上行1.3个百分点至51.7%；本月“抢生产”结束，生产指数相应下滑1.9个百分点至49.8%，企业采购量指数也回落2.1个百分点至48.9%，与往年10月类似。行业层面看，10月消费品行业PMI回落1.9个百分点至48.8%、降幅最大，也印证“抢生产”结束影响。 二是假期前置令需求提前释放、对10月形成透支，需求指标也有回落。 10月，制造业新订单指数回落1.1个百分点至49.4%。结构上，内需订单指数下滑1.1个百分点至49.5%，或源于长假带来的消费前置后、在节后趋于平淡；行业层面看，10月消费品制造业新订单指数较上月下降超过3个百分点至49%以下。此外，新出口订单指数回落1.3个百分点至48.7%，据中采称，背后是国外圣诞相关订单在上月集中释放后，10月内也有回落。高频层面看，10月港口外贸货运量也有回落。 此外，高油价的供给冲击、AI产业调整，也对10月制造业景气影响较大。 从行业结构看，高耗能行业PMI再度回落0.7个百分点至47.3%，纺织、非金属矿物制品等行业生产指数和新订单指数均低于临界点。或显示油价重新走高下供给冲击再显现。与此同时，高技术制造业景气继续回落，环比下行1.2个百分点至51.3%，装备制造业PMI也回落0.4个百分点至50.6%，有色压延行业的产需指数均低于临界点，或继续体现AI景气阶段性调整的影响。 非制造业PMI：景气虽有回落，但存量政策加速落地对基建领域仍有支撑，服务业PMI保持相对稳定。 10月，建筑业PMI回落2.3个百分点至48%；其中房屋建筑业景气水平回落至50%以下，而土木工程建筑业较上月上行、更多体现存量政策落地对基建领域的支撑。服务业景气仅下滑0.2个百分点至50%；结构上，十一假期对消费相关服务业的带动效应明显，铁路运输业商务活动指数升至60%以上，航空运输业商务活动指数升至54%以上，景区服务业和文体娱乐业PMI均升至53%以上。 展望后续：存量政策加速落地下，预计年内经济有望延续温和回升。 10月节日效应退坡下，制造业、非制造业景气均有回落；但制造业、建筑业、服务业生产经营预期分别保持在53.4%、52.3%、55.2%的较高水平。往后看，超强厄尔尼诺或将形成，虽然其带来的阶段性寒潮可能对内需形成短期扰动，但暖冬天气利好居民出行，或带动服务消费需求释放；同时存量政策加速落地，全球AI景气仍有上升空间，叠加前期盈利改善的滞后传导，预计四季度经济延续温和回升格局。 articles.title: 苹果收盘市值5.03万亿美元反超英伟达，重夺全球第一
articles.summary: 美股周五收盘，苹果市值报5.03万亿美元，从英伟达手中夺回全球市值最高公司的头衔。 投资者在AI开支担忧下，转而寻求这家iPhone制造商的相对安全性。 周五的收盘排名因此出现反转，苹果重新位居首位，英伟达退居第二。 收盘换位：苹果小跌，英伟达大跌 周五苹果股价下跌1.23%，收盘市值5.03万亿美元；英伟达收跌4.22%，收盘市值约4.93万亿美元。苹果跌幅明显小于英伟达，两者市值由此换位，苹果领先约0.1万亿美元。英伟达单日市值缩水约2170亿美元。 这是苹果自7月底短暂超越英伟达以来，首次再度登顶。 纳斯达克100指数10月下跌6.7%，为2025年3月以来最差单月，风险偏好承压。 AI开支担忧下的相对避风港 周五抛售的背景是，多家大型科技公司业绩令市场失望，包括英特尔、亚马逊，此前Alphabet、Meta等公司也出现类似情形。这再度引发对AI开支前景的担忧，而苹果大体上没有大规模投入AI基础设施。 对AI算力基础设施的重金投入能否回本，市场存在疑问，质疑AI投资能否在合理时间内产生足够的收入与利润。苹果相对克制的资本支出和强劲的现金流，使其被视为更具防御性的科技股。 年内涨幅与自由现金流 资本开支受控，让苹果成为“七巨头”中今年迄今表现最好的一只：年内上涨约27%，涨幅超过排名第二的英伟达的两倍以上。 现金流方面的差异同样明显。Alphabet、亚马逊等公司的自由现金流转为负值，更多转向债券市场融资，而利率上升推高了借贷成本。相比之下，苹果预计2026财年（截至9月30日）自由现金流将增长38%，达到1420亿美元。一边是现金流转负、融资成本上升，一边是现金流预计大幅增长，两者的对比构成了投资者偏好分化的背景。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 标普将Meta信用评级展望下调至负面，维持AA-，警告AI开支与自由现金流承压
articles.summary: 标普全球评级周五将Meta Platforms的AA-信用评级展望由稳定下调至负面，评级本身维持AA-不变。 标普的理由是AI相关高额资本开支推升杠杆，自由经营现金流承压，且Meta将AI投资变现的能力弱于同业。 标普表示，目前尚不清楚这些开支何时才会带来超过成本上升的重大收入。负面展望反映的是资本开支将维持高位多久、自由经营现金流将持续为负多久的不确定性。 同日美股科技股走弱，纳指收跌约3.5%，一度触及技术性回调。 开支攀升与杠杆抬升 标普预测，Meta今年资本开支约1400亿美元，2027年将逾2250亿美元。随着开支扩大，公司杠杆或最早在明年升至1.0倍以上，去年这一数字约为0.1倍。 标普同时指出，自由经营现金流（FOCF）存在压力和不确定性。在资本开支居高不下的情况下，现金流能否恢复，取决于AI投入何时转化为足够的收入。 本月早些时候，Meta披露未来开支承诺逾8000亿美元，其中近半与尚未启动的租赁有关，涉及数据中心和能源基础设施。 两年观察窗口，评级仍在高位 根据标普的规则，负面展望意味着未来约两年内评级可能被下调，但标普目前并未积极考虑立即下调。 AA-为第四高的投资级。即便未来下调一档，Meta仍处于高评级区间。标普此次的表态主要针对信用走势的方向，而非对当前信用质量的重新定级。 Meta回应不认同变现判断 Meta发言人Kamran Mumtaz表示，公司不认同标普对其AI变现能力的判断。他称：「我们看到前方有重大的产品与业务机会，支撑我们非常强劲的信用状况。」 在财报电话会上，Meta首席财务官Susan Li曾表示，公司预计将继续积极投资，以支持核心业务和新兴的AI计划。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 奥特曼：PC上装内存太浪费，最好留给AI数据中心
articles.summary: 「从全球资源配置的角度来看，让每个人把紧缺的 DRAM 囤在自己电脑里大部分时间闲置，是『相当糟糕』（quite terrible）的安排，内存应该集中到云端数据中心去。」 话都说到这份上了。 本周四在接受 YouTube 频道 Cheeky Pint 的采访时，OpenAI CEO 山姆・奥特曼（Sam Altman）全程喝着啤酒，气氛轻松地聊了聊 AI 大模型的本地推理，以及由此延伸出的家用电脑内存不足的问题，不经意间爆典了。 我们知道，目前全球 AI 浪潮引发的内存涨价，已经让 PC 和手机的价格暴涨了一圈，个人消费者早已难以承受。与此同时，各家内存大厂的产能扩张还要等一阵子。就在前沿 AI 公司吃下内存大头的同时，他们却已经开始讨论起个人电脑中的内存是否得到充分利用。 奥特曼提到一个假设，即人们能够在自己的电脑上运行本地人工智能，这些电脑可能是他们已经拥有的，也可能是因为 AI 大模型技术兴起，他们想要组装的。他认为这是一个糟糕的想法。 「从全球资源分配的角度来看，让每个人都把全球有限的 DRAM 内存闲置在自己的电脑里，而使用率只有 5%，这其实非常糟糕，」奥特曼说道。「如果你想在这种资源供应极其紧张的环境下工作，那么在云端就应该尽可能提高资源利用率。但不知为何，很多人的直觉却恰恰相反。」 如今，OpenAI 的主要业务基于在大规模数据中心运行的闭源模型，他为自家商业模式的辩护引发了 AI 社区的一片争论。 这也引发了不少人的担忧：未来我们可能更难拥有自己的硬件或软件，只能考虑去租用云端的智能体和计算机。 虽然普通 PC、手机和 AI 加速卡使用的内存并不相同，但它们的生产会竞争部分上游晶圆产能。奥特曼讨论的是全球 DRAM 的资源配置，要说到谁有资格决定内存产能用在哪里，大多数时候自然是下更大订单的那个用户。 奥特曼的部分观点基于数据中心建设不会放缓的假设。此外他还假设，全天候用于 AI 数据中心的内存比用于电子表格、网页浏览、游戏，甚至偶尔用于本地 AI 的内存更有价值。 其实这次的访谈很长，奥特曼聊的还包括这两周引爆全球恐慌的 PHP 漏洞、训练模型的沙箱化以及 AI 在数学领域的研究。 看看他主要说了些什么： AI 正在引爆漏洞潮 有关 PHP 超级巨大的漏洞，奥特曼的判断是：大模型发现漏洞的能力持续快速提升，而互联网上的代码面极其庞大，当人们开始系统性地用 AI 扫描所有代码，「我们会发现自己身处一个严重漏洞远超预期的世界」。他认为光打补丁不够，必须重构架构，路由器、操作系统、应用层都需要为「漏洞会越来越智能」的世界重新设计。两年前「重写整个技术栈」还像疯话，现在已出现要做全新 stack 的创业公司。 他罕见地做了行业自我批评：「我不认为我们很好地向人们解释了，为什么这项技术所有潜在的下行风险是值得的。」他说 AI 行业的叙事是糟糕的销售话术，一边承诺治愈癌症、降低成本，一边又描绘失业、失控、需要强力监管的未来。他重申 OpenAI 坚持迭代部署（iterative deployment）、对抗能力悬置（capability overhang），理由是不能让「旧金山几平方英里的人做所有决定」。 当被问及能否给模型建一个「最高安全级别的监狱」，奥特曼给出了悲观回答：沙箱只在一定程度内有效，监控（包括思维链审查和激活监控）能再进一步，但最终必须高度信任对齐。他反问道，面对一个比最聪明的安全研究员还聪明百万倍、能发现人类尚不懂的新科学的模型，你真敢信任那个沙箱吗？ 他明确说自己讨厌「agent swarms（蜂群）」这个词，因为 swarm 让人联想到蝗虫，坚持叫 agent teams（智能体团队），并认为团队之间互相制衡的属性，恰好对应靠多元主义实现鲁棒性的机制，是值得推进的安全方向。 智力爆炸与科学发现的代价 奥特曼勾勒了一条曲线：GPT-4 时代，往单个问题上有效投入 1 美元算力都难；思维链（chain of thought）让模型能「用力思考」，如今我们却可以把整支智能体团队并行上万次。普通用户和最先进用户之间的使用差距，正在不断拉大。 关于 OpenAI 内部如何分配算力，他说员工享有很大自由度，但从不奖励高 token 消耗，「token 排行榜高其实有点丢人，肯定不是晋升理由」。纳维 - 斯托克斯（Navier-Stokes）方程的证明被他拿来当案例：单个证明约耗资 1000 万美元，期间「失控了一周」，因为当时大家对智能体团队的扩展律一无所知。但他预计一年后用更聪明的模型和方法，1/100 的成本就能重做。 他还罕见地流露了情绪：当时的情况真是绝了，某个新模型内部上线的周末，大家把各种最棘手的难题抛给这个模型，而它竟然都能一一解决。人们原本根本没指望模型能做到这些。大家共同见证了许多人学术生涯中最难攻克的科研难题被这个模型一个接一个地解决了，而且涵盖了多个不同的领域，那场面简直令人惊叹。 「有两晚我几乎彻夜未眠，因为实在太兴奋了，根本睡不着。我们后来发表的很多成果，其实就是当时解决的那些难题。」 奥特曼当时感到无比兴奋和快乐，同时也涌现出一种意想不到的忧伤、惆怅，以及一种「某个时代正在终结」的感觉。不止是怀旧，还有一种对于对人类科学家们「朝闻道，夕死可矣」的共情。他坚持人类理应获得基础知识，但行业欠这些领域的从业者一个解决方案。 虽然现在谈论超级智能还为时尚早，不过奥特曼认为万亿个小超人类，胜过一个万亿 IQ： "I would much rather intuitively have a trillion AIs of slightly superhuman intelligence join society than one AI of one trillion IQ join society." 「直觉上，我更愿意让一万亿个略具超人类智能的 AI 加入社会，而不是一个万亿 IQ 的 AI 加入社会。」 他的论证是：社会的强大鲁棒性来自大量成员互相制衡、协作，「单脑」世界没有这种韧性。但他强调这不会自动发生，必须主动推动。 市场调节，到 AI 时代玩不转了？ 有关全球内存紧缺的问题，奥特曼介绍了 OpenAI 的布局：自研芯片（提升每瓦智能性能）、自建数据中心、机器人项目，以及一个更大胆的概念「自我复制的数据中心」，要用 AI 控制机器人去运营晶圆厂、造涡轮和太阳能板、建数据中心。他表示「这已在我们掌握之中」。 谈到「市场自己调节」为何迟迟不兑现，他认为当前的进展很糟糕，并给出内存厂商的行为逻辑：这个行业长期是投 200 亿美元 capex 赚 19 亿的苦生意，历史上多次有巨头因过度建厂而差点破产。如今每家一年能赚约 1000 亿美元自由现金流，但惨痛记忆让他们扩产极度保守。他由此断言「看不见的手现在失灵了」。 他区分了芯片产业的两类能力：光刻「地球上似乎只有一家公司知道怎么做」，但芯片设计（最终送给晶圆厂的文件）已是 AI 的绝佳用武之地。 谈到递归自我改进（RSI）的真实水平，奥特曼表示，现在模型能完成「找 5% 计算效率提升」这类任务，但还没有人知道如何让 AI 发现像 transformer 那样级别的新架构，缺的是更聪明的模型。他甚至预告，社会可能需要在一段时间内同意限制单模型的智商，「若未来的进展不足，那将源于这个决定，而非 AI 做研究的能力」。 他亮出了自己的通缩信仰：当前每 GW 领先 AI 算力的 5 年总拥有成本约 700 亿美元，若能降到 200 亿会更理想，同时模型每年还要再提升 10 倍性能。实现的路径是让能源更便宜、压缩「从沙子到产出 token」之间层层堆叠的毛利。 针对企业的 token 预算焦虑，他认为当前更普遍的问题是 AI 用得不够多，而不是用太多。 个人智能体怎么定价？ 关于最近火热的个人智能体产品（如 Muse），奥特曼当前的判断是「Macintosh 时刻还没有到来」。人们喜欢这些产品，但还没到「无法想象没有它的生活」，赢家的形态会像现在的产品，但「it'll just work」，可靠、能接住更复杂的任务。computer use 的猫鼠游戏，他认为最终会收敛在「你有权让 AI 代表你操作自己的电脑」的程度。 有关智能体的商业化方式，奥特曼认为，企业死守自己产品里的 AI 弹窗和 HTML，担心失去客户关系，但消费者想在自己的主聊天应用里面让 AI 代办一切。他认为真正的护城河来自品牌、选品和履约网络，而非 HTML。他主动自曝说：自己 10 次有 10 次选 Amazon Pay，哪怕价格更高，并盛赞亚马逊的履约网络，同时承认 ChatGPT 内的合作平台做得还不够好。他还把所有网页表单称为「假工作」（fake work），并把当下类比为当年的 App Store 时代。 也正是因为如此，在设计定价时，OpenAI 差点学 AWS 按任务报价、彻底抛弃 token 计费的方式，但遭到了客户们的强烈反对：「我需要知道自己在为什么付钱」，哪怕付更多也要 token 这种可理解的单位。 本文来源： 机器之心 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 长安汽车短期业绩承压，部分新能源平台已盈利
articles.summary: 10月30日晚，长安汽车披露2026年三季报。第三季度，公司营业收入362.5亿元，同比下降14.17%；归母净亏损7.58亿元，扣非后归母净亏损9.52亿元。公司同期发布的经营信息显示，三季度营收环比增长10.1%。 在整体业绩承压的同时，部分新能源平台已出现盈利进展。从长安汽车方面了解到，目前启源A06、Q06所在平台已经实现盈利，后续同平台新车型的边际成本将持续降低。 对于前三季度的净利润变化，长安汽车在财报中列出的主要原因是销量下降、原材料涨价及汇兑损失增加。持续的研发支出也反映在报表中：前三季度研发费用为52.61亿元，较上年同期的50.39亿元增加约4.4%。 在长安汽车总裁叶沛看来，公司正处于新旧增长动能切换的阶段。他表示，长安正在推动收入结构和盈利基础发生变化：市场上，从国内单一支撑转向国内与海外共同支撑；产品上，从过去以燃油车营收和利润为主，转向智慧新能源与节能汽车共同支撑。 这一调整也涉及产品开发的取舍。叶沛提到，公司持续投入海外布局、车型开发和前沿技术研发，同时推进产品结构升级，在规模上做取舍，并计划精简产品品种。按照他的判断，走出这一轮调整周期，关键在于构建新的增长逻辑。 “长期投入、短期承压是我们主动的战略选择。”长安汽车执行副总裁张晓宇称，公司正在统一硬件接口、提高复用率，通过规模摊薄硬件成本，再依靠软件和AI形成不同产品的体验差异。 产品结构的变化已经有了相应的经营数据。长安汽车前三季度新能源产品中，10万元以上产品占比接近70%；第三季度单车收入达到10.1万元，环比提高0.5万元。智能化配置方面，启源Q06 Ultra版选装率接近50%。 海外市场则是另一项布局重点。公司披露，第三季度海外销量同比增长64%，创下新高，预计全年海外销量将突破100万辆。前三季度，长安汽车海外战略资源累计投入54.6亿元，主要用于销售资源、人工及日常运营等。 对于海外增长的来源，长安汽车也在进行产品本地化适配、新市场拓展，以及海外团队、分公司和合作伙伴资源逐步转化为销量。 智能化业务也在推进新的资本安排。长安汽车同期公告，全资子公司重庆长安科技有限责任公司拟通过增资扩股引入投资者，并在产权交易所预挂牌征集意向投资方，具体投资者、增资金额及股权比例尚待确定。 按照公告，此次引资旨在推动“北斗天枢”智能化战略落地，支持长安科技推进市场化运营，加快产品迭代与产业化。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 财报炸裂，但闪迪隔夜为何暴跌？
articles.summary: 闪迪交出全面超预期的财报，股价却在周五美股盘前一度暴跌8%。问题出在它的日本晶圆厂合作伙伴铠侠（Kioxia）：后者给出的利润指引不及预期，并警告AI推动的闪存涨价潮正在降温。 闪迪周四盘后的成绩单几乎挑不出毛病：营收和每股收益超预期，毛利率85%，指引高于华尔街预期，另追加50亿美元回购并宣布1拆8拆股。但股价盘后纹丝不动。 美东时间周五5:54，彭博报道了铠侠的指引，闪迪盘前最多跌至1197.57美元，较周三1419美元的高点回落16%，美光科技随之走低。 有分析指出：“在存储行业，唯一重要的数字是二阶导。”换句话说，当下市场关心的是价格涨得多快。 数据显示，NAND闪存平均售价在截至9月的三个月里上涨25%左右，前一季度的涨幅是70%。 铠侠：价格飙升正开始趋于平稳 铠侠预计本季度营业利润为2万亿日元（约127亿美元），远低于市场预期的2.35万亿日元。 刚结束的9月季度依然亮眼：营业利润同比增长22倍，达到1.99万亿日元，与预期一致；营收约2.48万亿日元，环比增长40%。公司还首次派发中期股息，每股90日元。 麻烦在下一季度。按上述分析的测算，2万亿日元的指引意味着12月季度营业利润环比几乎零增长，而9月季度环比增长了57%，市场一致预期原本还计入了约18%的增幅。彭博的Takashi Mochizuk分析称，铠侠的展望表明，过去一年左右史无前例的价格飙升正开始趋于平稳。 换句话说，价格还在涨，但速度只有三个月前的三分之一左右。分析认为，对于按“曲线只会越来越陡”定价的股票来说，这就足以构成利空。 客户也开始吃不消。据媒体报道，铠侠高管已警告不要过度涨价，以免疏远客户。英特尔周五预计，今年PC出货量将下降约12%，2027年再降约10%，“存储供应受限”是原因之一；公司把“出人意料的严重PC调整”归咎于存储价格，股价盘前暴跌25%。 抛售随即扩散。摩根大通市场情报团队称，存储ETF（DRAM）盘前下跌5.6%，市场对AI变现的担忧再起，整个半导体板块承压。就在两天前，股指期货还在“SK海力士带动的存储狂热”中上涨。 铠侠自己的股价在财报前已较6月高点下跌约60%。高盛的Jay Narain指出，即便如此，其自2024年12月IPO以来的累计回报仍有2400%。 闪迪：超了市场预期，没超买方预期 单看数字，闪迪这一季很扎实。据高盛TMT交易台汇总，闪迪营收110.3亿美元，高于市场预期的107.4亿美元；毛利率85.1%，略高于市场预期的84.9%；非GAAP每股收益49.51美元，高于市场预期的46.73美元。 问题在指引的细节里。闪迪下季度营收指引中值124亿美元、非GAAP每股收益55至57美元，高于市场一致预期的120.8亿美元和52.94美元，却明显低于高盛预测的135.5亿美元和59.71美元。分析认为，高盛的数字大致代表了买方私下的“耳语预期”，也就是机构投资者真正期待的水平。 管理层对数据中心业务相当乐观。闪迪称，数据中心已占行业比特需求的一半左右，2020年这一比例约为20%；公司预计到2030年，KV缓存（大模型推理时存放中间计算结果的缓存）将占AI数据中心市场的约35%，2027年数据中心将占NAND市场的55%以上。 管理层还说，多家客户“此前低估了自己的NAND需求”，闪迪会按“重新谈定的更高价格”供货。至于能高多少，与闪迪共用晶圆厂的铠侠刚刚给出了答案：比之前少得多。 这一幕8月已上演过一次，当时闪迪同样全面超预期，股价照样下跌。高盛分析师Jim Schneider的财报点评显示，长期协议目前覆盖闪迪2027财年计划比特产能的约50%、2028财年的65%，与8月持平，尽管其间又多签了两份（迄今与8家客户签署10份协议）。 长期协议约定了价格底线，能起到缓冲作用。但上述分析指出，这意味着明年仍有一半的产能要随合约市场价格浮动，而铠侠刚刚说明了合约市场的方向。 Schneider仍然看多。他认为NAND市场“在可预见的未来供给增量非常有限”，将2026至2028年每股收益预测上调约7%，并指出公司回购授权仍剩105亿美元。他周四晚间写道：“预计强劲的季度业绩过后，股价将温和上涨。”这一判断只维持到了周五凌晨5:54。 周期拐点，还是喘口气？ NAND有两种价格：现货价是即期市场的成交价，反应快；合约价由厂商与大客户定期重新谈定，调整有滞后。上述分析早在6月25日存储交易见顶当天就指出，现货价从3月起已停止上涨。此后合约价又涨了两个季度，如今两者的时间差正在收窄。 供给仍在增加。铠侠计划未来六年与闪迪在日本投入逾5万亿日元扩产，部分资金将来自明年在美国发行ADR，募资规模可能至少100亿美元。美光正在新加坡建设240亿美元的NAND工厂；长江存储已拿下全球NAND市场13%的份额，与闪迪持平；DRAM龙头长鑫存储9月也进入闪存市场。 三星的NAND业务同样逊于预期。高盛的Giuni Lee称其NAND利润“略低于我们的预期（比特出货量和平均售价均略低）”。 存储涨价已传导至PC、手机和服务器，高盛的Rich Privorotsky指出，英特尔的PC业务正因“存储通胀推高硬件成本而萎缩”。NAND涨价放缓对CPI和PC厂商是好消息，对一直按涨价逻辑定价的存储股则是坏消息。 空头们分析称，存储本质上是周期行业，过去一年却说服自己相信是结构性的。现货价3月见顶，合约价涨幅从70%降至25%左右，铠侠一边指引利润持平、一边投入5万亿日元扩产，又因最大的买家买不起芯片而削减出货。另据彭博，大型科技公司7500亿美元的AI支出正与核心业务增长放缓相撞。不少投资者认为，本应消化这些新增产能的超大规模云厂商，可能也会开始更强硬地议价。 多头则认为：季度涨幅25%左右依然是罕见的强势市场，数据中心需求具有结构性，铠侠管理层可能是有意保守。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: AI股重挫而等权标普逆势涨1.2%，必需消费领涨并一度创新高
articles.summary: 周五早盘，AI股再遭重挫，纳斯达克100指数下跌3%，等权重标普500指数却逆势上涨约1.2%。指数之下的分化表明，跌幅高度集中在大型科技股和AI相关股票上。 标普500指数当时下跌1.5%。英特尔录得有记录以来最大日内跌幅，AI主导的抛售让本周的科技股跌势进一步加深；高盛追踪美国上市AI概念股的GS Broad AI US Index下跌4.7%。 防御板块则受到追捧。必需消费是标普500表现最好的板块，上涨1.64%，板块指数在纽约午盘前一度创下纪录新高。 财报撑起必需消费 标普1500必需消费指数盘中最多上涨2.3%，临近美东时间11点回吐部分涨幅。领涨的是两家刚交出亮眼财报的公司。 高露洁-棕榄盘前一度上涨5.5%，开盘后涨约2.5%。这家家庭及个人护理用品公司的利润和总销售额均超过彭博一致预期。尽管美国及北美市场表现偏软，但已在改善，强劲的利润和业绩指引占了上风。 零食生产商亿滋国际盘前涨幅略超7%，午盘前上涨约3%。公司第三季度业绩超出预期，主要靠稳健的销量增长。 剔除AI股，标普500本月有望涨6% 瑞银的Mark Paski表示，剔除AI股的标普500成分股本月有望上涨6%，为2022至2023年AI交易开始升温以来的最佳月度表现。 他认为，随着利率走低、企业盈利保持韧性，上涨正从少数龙头扩散到更多股票。第三季度财报季初期，78%的公司每股收益超出市场预期，但利润率仍是消费类公司的关键问题。 可选消费公司对需求的判断也偏乐观。希尔顿预计，旗下酒店体系的增长势头将延续至今年余下时间并进入2027年；皇家加勒比称，2027年的预订进度领先于历史水平，价格也更高；捷蓝航空则表示，9月的强劲表现延续到了10月。Paski提醒，更大的不确定性仍在利润和利润率。 “如果市场广度继续改善，除了近期的领涨股，基本面更强的消费类股票也会越来越具备配置价值。”他写道。 从周五的盘面看，投资者是在把资金从AI交易挪向防御类股票，并没有恐慌性地全面撤离股市。即便AI相关交易遭到重创，普通个股依然站得住。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。
